article.title: The White House is betting the election on a theory of skewed polls 🚩🚩🚩🚩🚩
article.subtitle: The polls may be off in either direction. But banking on an error in your favor is usually a red flag.

extraction.summary: Silver argues that the Biden White House is engaging in 'poll unskewing' in March 2024, when Biden trails Trump nationally and by more in swing states. He reviews 2008-2022 to show that Democrats were rarely behind and that polls were mostly accurate. He notes that 2016 and 2020 polls overrated Democrats and that 2022 polls were historically accurate. The central forecasting lesson is that the direction of polling error is historically unpredictable, so banking on an error in your favor is a red flag. Two FiveThirtyEight tables cover statistical bias and weighted-average error of polls in the final 21 days of races since 1998, with pollsters weighted by one over the square root of their poll count. The article is marked as paywalled, but the full text appears to be present.

findings.statement: The direction of polling error has historically been impossible to predict in advance. Conventional wisdom has usually been wrong when it tried to guess which party polls would underrate, so forecasts should treat systematic polling error as symmetric around zero rather than assuming error in one party's favor.
findings.rationale: In 2012 and 2022 insiders expected Democrats to underperform their polls but they outperformed. In 2014 and 2016 the reverse happened.
findings.evidence_quote: it's historically been impossible to predict the direction in which polls are wrong, and the conventional wisdom has usually been wrong when it tried to guess.

findings.statement: The FiveThirtyEight polling-bias and polling-error metrics use polls whose median field date falls in the final 21 days before the election. They include presidential, Senate, House and gubernatorial general elections since 1998, plus special elections and runoffs, and exclude pollsters banned by FiveThirtyEight.

findings.statement: In the FiveThirtyEight error and bias tables, each poll is weighted by 1/sqrt(n), where n is the number of polls its pollster conducted for that type of election in that cycle. This prevents prolific pollsters from dominating the averages.

quantities.name: poll weight
quantities.value: 1/sqrt(n)
quantities.context: n = polls by that pollster for that election type in that cycle

findings.statement: Statistical bias in the FiveThirtyEight table is calculated only for elections in which the top two finishers were a Republican and a Democrat. It is therefore not calculated for presidential primaries.

For presidential primary polling-error calculations, FiveThirtyEight excludes the following polls: New Hampshire primary polls taken before the Iowa caucuses; other states' primary polls taken before the New Hampshire primary; polls where the leader or runner-up dropped out before the primary; polls where any candidate receiving at least 15% dropped out; and polls where any combination of candidates receiving at least 25% dropped out.

findings.statement: There is no clear long-term trend in polling accuracy. Polls were pretty good in 2012, 2018 and 2022, quite bad in 2016 and 2020, and in between in 2014. Silver accepts a mild prior that polling is getting worse because of declining response rates, but rejects a binary 'polls work vs. polls are broken' framing.
findings.rationale: Poor polling years also occurred before the modern era (1998, 1980, 1948).
findings.evidence_quote: If you want to start with the prior that polling is getting worse a priori because of declining response rates, I don't have a big problem with that.

findings.statement: Polls taken in March of an election year are historically not very reliable predictors of November results. One reason is that campaigns have time to change course and tweak strategies that are not working.
findings.rationale: Campaigns can respond to bad polling.
findings.evidence_quote: one reason polls in March aren't historically all that reliable is because campaigns have the opportunity to change course and tweak a strategy that isn't working.

findings.statement: Candidates' relative favorability ratings predict election results extremely well; Silver calls this 'almost axiomatic'. Biden's stronger 2020 favorability versus Clinton's in 2016 explains why he won where she lost. Trump's 2024 head-to-head lead follows predictably from Biden's favorability now being markedly worse than Trump's.
findings.evidence_quote: You can, in fact, predict election results extremely well by knowing each candidate's favorability ratings; in fact, this is almost axiomatic.

findings.statement: Special and off-year elections, such as the 2023 races, are low-turnout contests that may say little about a presidential general election, especially when the president is not on the ballot. The NYT poll replicated Democrats' strong performance in such contests while still showing Biden trailing Trump.
findings.rationale: Voter concerns specific to Biden, such as his age, would not show up in races where he is not on the ballot.
findings.evidence_quote: it's not clear how much one should take away from these low-turnout races.

findings.statement: In 2022, polls of the House popular vote were nearly exactly right and polls were highly accurate in aggregate. Democrats were very slightly overestimated overall. Forecast models had Republicans favored in the House and the Senate as close, which the results reasonably matched. 'Red wave' predictions came from pundits and defied the polling averages.
findings.evidence_quote: it was a way better year for the polling industry than the takes industry.

findings.statement: In both elections with Trump on the ballot (2016 and 2020), polls overstated the Democrat. Biden in 2020 considerably underperformed his polls but held on in tipping-point states such as Georgia and Wisconsin because his lead was large.
findings.evidence_quote: that's what happened to the Democrat the only other two times that Trump was on the ballot in 2016 and 2020.

findings.statement: Silver suggests that pollsters may compensate for low phone response rates by moving online and doing more modeling and massaging of their data, even if this departs from the traditional hands-off 'gold standard' approach.
findings.evidence_quote: pollsters may be able to compensate for this by doing more massaging and modeling with their data, even this means a retreat from the traditional, hands-off, "gold standard" approach to polling.

findings.statement: In 2020, conventional wisdom was more equivocal about Biden than the polls were, but Biden was still the favorite in prediction markets.
findings.rationale: Lingering caution after the 2016 polling miss.
findings.evidence_quote: Biden was the favorite in prediction markets.

findings.statement: In early 2024, Biden trailed Trump by a wider margin in swing-state polling than nationally, implying an Electoral College disadvantage for Democrats. If the election were held then, Trump would be favored, with Biden within striking distance only through a systematic polling error.
findings.evidence_quote: Biden generally trails Trump by a wider margin in swing state polling.

political_insights.insight: March 2024 marked the first time since 2004 that Democrats trailed in presidential polls. Obama in 2008 led except briefly after the Palin pick and the RNC, Obama in 2012 outperformed his polls, and Clinton in 2016 and Biden in 2020 led throughout.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Campaign and media reactions to trailing polls may produce motivated 'unskewing' that forecasters should ignore.

political_insights.insight: Biden's approval rating was 38 percent in March 2024, evidence that voters had soured on him.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Low incumbent approval feeds into the fundamentals of a presidential forecast.

political_insights.insight: 2022 was one of the historically stronger midterms for the president's party. Democrats expanded their Senate margin and narrowly lost the House. Abortion probably mattered more than election denialism.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: The midterm penalty is not uniform; issue salience can blunt it.

political_insights.insight: Democracy-related issues poll low as most-important issues. In October 2020 Gallup polling, 30% named COVID, 14% the economy, 5% unifying the country and 2% elections. Voters compartmentalize January 6 as bad but well-litigated, and a near-catastrophe does not move most voters like an actual catastrophe.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Be skeptical that campaign messaging on democracy will shift the polls substantially.

political_insights.insight: Silver doubts other 2020 Democrats (Sanders, Harris, Warren, Buttigieg, Bloomberg, Klobuchar) would have won given Biden's narrow tipping-point margins, citing ideology, inexperience or weak retail politics.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Candidate quality can matter at the margin in close elections.

political_insights.insight: Biden led the 2020 Democratic primary polls consistently until Iowa and again after South Carolina. Media underrated him on vibes rather than polls.

Evan Osnos New Yorker profile of Biden, 2024

open_questions: How the Silver Bulletin 2024 model translates historical polling bias and error into the size and distribution of its simulated systematic error.
How favorability ratings, as opposed to head-to-head polls, enter the forecast, if at all.
How much early-cycle (March) polls are discounted relative to fundamentals in the 2024 model.
